title: Nitriensis
description: Contains: Gospel of Luke
location: Monastery of St. Mary Deipara, Egypt

title: Porphyrianus
description: The manuscript was discovered by Tischendorf in 1862 at Saint Petersburg in the possession of the Archimandrite Porphyrius Uspensky, who allowed him to take it to Leipzig to decipher lower script. Contains: Acts (lacking Acts 1:1–2:13), Pauline Epistles (lacking Romans 2:16–3:4; 8:32–9:10; 11:23–12:1; 1 Cor. 7:15–17; 12:23–13:5; 14:23–39; 2 Cor. 2:13–16; Col. 3:16–4:8; 1 Thes. 3:5–4:17), General Epistles (lacking 1 John 3:20–5:1; Jude 4–15), Revelation (lacking Rev. 16:12–17:1; 19:21–20:9; 22:6–end).

title: Uncial 0166
description: The manuscript was found in Egypt. It is the last uncial manuscript added to the list of New Testament manuscripts by Gregory. The codex currently is housed at the University of Heidelberg. Contains: Acts 28:30-31; James 1:11

title: Uncial 0165
description: The manuscript was added to the list of New Testament manuscripts by C. R. Gregory in 1909. The codex currently is housed at the Berlin State Museums in Berlin. Contains: Acts 3:24-4:13,17-20

title: Uncial 068
description: The manuscript was found in 1847 in the monastery at Nitrian Desert and brought to London. Contains: John 13:16-17, 19-20, 23-24, 26-27, 16:7-9, 12-13, 15-16, 18-19

title: Uncial 0131
description: The leaves of this manuscript were discovered by William White in 1857 in book of Gregory of Nazianzus. The codex came from the Athos. Since 1861 they are stored separately from this book, on the order of Henry Bradshaw. Contains: Mark 7-9

title: Uncial 050
description: Possibly the codex was written in Athos peninsula. The Moscow fragment was brought from the Dionysiou monastery. The fragment John 4:7-14 (three leaves) was discovered by Bradshaw in 1863. The codex is divided and located in four places. 2 leaves are housed at the Εθνική Βιβλιοθήκη in Athens, 7 leaves in the Dionysiou monastery in Athos, 7 leaves in the State Historical Museum, and 3 leaves in the Christ Church. Contains: John

title: Uncial 0274
description: After discovery in Nubia (possibly Qasr Ibrim) it was held in Cairo. Currently the codex is housed at the Coptic Museum in Cairo. Contains: Mark 6:56-7:4, 6-9, 13-17, 19-23, 28, 34, 8:3, 8-11, 9:20-22, 26-41, 9:43-10:1, 17-22

title: Boernerianus
description: The codex was probably written by an Irish monk in the Abbey of St. Gall, Switzerland between 850-900 A.D. In 1670 it was in the hands of P. Junius at Leiden. The codex got its name from its first German owner, University of Leipzig professor Christian Frederick Boerner, who bought it in the Dutch Republic in the year 1705. Rettig thought that Codex Sangallensis is a part of the same book as the Codex Boernerianus,[ which some other scholars also believe. During World War II, the codex suffered severely from water damage. Thus the facsimile as published in 1909 provides the most legible text. Contains: Pauline epistles (lacking Romans 1:1-4, 2:17-24, 1 Cor. 3:8-16, 6:7-14, Col. 2:1-8, Philem. 21-25, Hebrews)

title: Uncial 0133
description: The manuscript was discovered in 1881 by Abbott and Mahaffy in Blenheim Palace. Gregory in 1883 found two leaves more. It is a palimpsest, the upper text is a menaeon (see Uncial 094, Uncial 0120). Formerly to this codex were included Uncial 0271, 0272 and 0273. The text of menaion was written by Archbishop of Selymeria in 1431. Contains: Matthew 1:1-14, 5:3-19, 23:9-25:30, 25:43-26:26, 26:50-27:16; Mark 1:1-43, 2:21-5:1, 5:29-6:22, 10:51-11:13

title: Uncial 0163
description: The manuscript was found in Al-Bashnasa (modern name of Oxhyrrincus) . The text of the manuscript was published in 1908 by B. P. Grenfell and A. S. Hunt. Contains: Revelation 16:17-20

title: Uncial 047
description: The earliest history of the manuscript is unknown. It was formerly held in the monastery of St. Andrew on Athos Peninsula, where scholar Caspar René Gregory discovered it in 1886, and provided the first description of it.It was brought by Thomas Whittemore to the United States after being purchased by athlete, investment banker and philanthropist Robert Garrett. It was donated by Garrett in 1942 to the Princeton University Library in Princeton, New Jersey. Contains: Gospels

title: Uncial 054
description: A.k.a. Codex Barberini. It was found in the 17th century by Cardinal Francesco Barberini (hence name of the codex). Contains: John 16:13-19:41

title: Dublinensis
description: The history of the codex is unknown until the underlying text was discovered by John Barrett in 1787, under some cursive writing. It is named "Dublinensis" because it currently resides at Dublin University. Contains: Matthew

title: Uncial 0220
description: A.k.a. the Wyman fragment, it was purchased in Cairo in 1950 by Leland C. Wyman, a professor of biology at Boston University. Later part of it was bought by Martin Schøyen and now part of it is housed in the Martin Schøyen Collection in Oslo, and part in London. In 2012 this text was purchased at a Sotheby's auction by the Green Collection.The text was published by William Hatch in the Harvard Theological Review in 1952. Contains: Romans 4:23–5:3, 5:8–13

title: Claromontanus
description: Uncial 06 a.k.a Codex Claromontanus is a Greek-Latin diglot. Purchased in Clermont-en-Beauvaisis, Oise, in the Picardy region north of Paris, by Theodore Beza, who lived in the 1500s. Two palimpsest leaves (nos. 162 and 163) are overwritten on fragments of the Phaethon of Euripides, faintly legible under the Christian text. Beza was the first to examine it, and he included notes of some of its readings in his editions of the New Testament. The manuscript was examined by Johann Jakob Griesbach and Constantin von Tischendorf, who edited the Greek text of the codex. Paul Sabatier edited the Latin text of the codex. Johann Gottfried Jakob Hermann published in 1821 the palimpsest text of the leaves 162–163. A stichometric catalogue of the Old Testament and New Testament canon, known as the Catalogus Claromontanus, of uncertain date, has been inserted in the codex. The list omits Philippians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, and Hebrews, but includes several works no longer considered canonical: Epistle of Barnabas, The Shepherd of Hermas, Acts of Paul, and Revelation of Peter. The two epistles of Peter are listed as if they were epistles of Paul to Peter ("ad Petrum"). The Epistle to the Hebrews follows after this catalogue. Contains: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews

title: Zacynthius
description: The early history of the manuscript is unknown. In 1821 it was brought by General Colin Macaulay to England from the Greek island Zakynthos in the Ionian Sea, after being presented to him by Prince Comuto (Antonios Dimitriou Komoutos, 1748-1833) a former President of the Septinsular Republic. Comuto inscribed the Codex to Macaulay as a token of his esteem. On his return to England Macaulay presented the Codex to British and Foreign Bible Society, which then placed it in its library (Mss 24) in London. Contains: Luke

title: Cyprius
description: The early history of the codex is unknown. It was brought from Cyprus to the Colbert Library in Paris in 1673,  whence it passed into its present locality in the National Library of France. Contains: Gospels

title: Washingtonianus
description: Codex Washingtonianus, a.k.a. Codex Washingtonensis, Codex Freerianus, the Washington Manuscript of the Gospels, The Freer Gospel and The Freer Codex. During a trip to Egypt in December 1906, Charles Lang Freer bought the manuscript from an antiques dealer in Cairo, along with three other manuscripts.  Biblical scholar Bruce M. Metzger states: "It is the only Greek Gospel manuscript of early date of which we know provenance. Though the exact spot in Egypt where it was found is not known, there are indications that it came from a monastery in the neighbourhood of the Pyramids." It has been described as one of the "more important majuscule manuscripts discovered during the 20th century" and "a highly valuable manuscript." In the Gospel of Mark, it shares several distinctive readings with the early 3rd century papyrus, the Chester Beatty codex of the Gospels and Acts (𝔓45).  It is considered to be the third oldest Gospel parchment codex in the world. Contains: Gospels

title: Uncial 0196
description: The manuscript was discovered in 1929 by Hatch. According to him the manuscript was written by Egyptian or Palestinian hand. The codex used to be housed at the National Museum of Damascus. The manuscript is not accessible. Contains: Matthew 5:1-11; Luke 24:26-33

title: Uncial 0171
description: The manuscript was found in 1903–1905 in Hermopolis Magna.[8] The text was first published by the Società Italiana in Florence in 1912. Contains: Matthew 10:17-23,25-32; Luke 22:44-50,52-56,61,63-64

title: Boreelianus
description: The earliest history of the manuscript is unknown. The codex is named after Johann Boreel (1577–1629), Dutch Ambassador at the Court of James I of England. There is no record of when Boreel obtained the codex, but it is generally believed that he brought it to the Netherlands from one of his travels to the Middle East. After Johann Boreel's death in 1629, the codex itself was in private hands. Boreel's library was sold in 1632, but the manuscript may not have been among the items for sale. It could have remained in the possession of Boreel's family, for example, in the hands of his younger brother, the theologian Adam Boreel (1602–54).The codex resurfaced almost two centuries later, in 1823, and was identified as the Boreelianus by the Utrecht professor Jodocus Heringa (1765–1840). The manuscript was now in the private hands of Johannes Michaelis Roukens in Arnhem. In a letter of 11 March 1830, Roukens explained that the manuscript had been in the possession of his father, Arend Anton Roukens, who had inherited it from his father, Johannes Michaelis Roukens. Contains: Gospels

title: Uncial 075
description: The manuscript was written by monk Sabbas. Formerly it was held in Kosinitza. C. R. Gregory saw the manuscript in 1886. Contains: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon

title: Uncial 0118
description: The codex was found in the end of the 19th century by J. Rendel Harris in the Saint Catherine's Monastery,[3] in Sinai peninsula, where is located to the present day. Contains: Matthew 11:27-28
location: Saint Catherine's Monastery, Mt. Sinai, Egypt

title: Uncial 0169
description: A.k.a. the Princeton fragment, edited in 1911 by Grenfell and Hunt. The codex currently is housed at the Princeton Theological Seminary Contains: Revelation 3:19-4:3

title: Uncial 0308
description: A.k.a. Oxyrhynchus 4500, is cataloged among the Oxyrhynchus Papyri as P. Oxy. 4500, and is now part of the Sackler Library collection in Oxford. Contains: Revelation 11:15-16; 11:17-18

title: Uncial 0162
description: A.k.a. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 847 or P.Oxy. 847. The text was first published by Grenfell and Hunt in The Oxyrhynchus Papyri in 1908. Contains: John 2:11–22

title: Uncial 0206
description: The manuscript was found in Oxyrhynchus by B. P. Grenfell and A. S. Hunt. They published a description of its text. The manuscript was added to the list of the New Testament manuscripts by textual critic and theologian Ernst von Dobschütz in 1933. Contains: 1 Peter 5:5-13

title: Codex Coislinianus
description: A.k.a. Uncial 015, is known for its colophon following Titus, in which a scribe named Euthalius states he wrote the volume in stichoi and collated it against a Caesarean exemplar written by Pamphilus; hence the alternative name Codex Euthalianus.The codex was probably written in the 6th century at the library in Caesarea, later coming into the possession of the monastery of the Great Lavra on Mount Athos, but its value appears to have been overlooked. Leaves of the codex were used as raw material for the production of new volumes. In 975 some leaves, now known as Fragmenta Mosquensia, were used to cover a volume of Gregory Nazianzen at Mount Athos. In the 12th century Fragmenta Taurinensia were used in Nicetas' catenae to the Psalterium, in 1218 another part, now named as Fragmenta Coisliniana, were used with the same purpose.[16]As a result, leaves of the codex were scattered in several places of the monastery, from where they were collected on several occasions by people from France, Russia, and Italy. The first was Pierre Séguier (1588–1672), who bought 14 leaves which, known later as Fragmenta Coisliniana, and became a part of the Fonds Coislin. They were held in Saint-Germain-des-Prés. In 1715 Bernard de Montfaucon published text of these 14 leaves.[17] He made a few mistakes corrected by Tischendorf (in 1865). Tischendorf observed in Paris additional passage. Montfaucon used the manuscript for his palaeographical studies. After the fire of St. Germain-des-Prés in 1793 only 12 leaves were found, the other two have been transferred to Saint Petersburg.[19] From 1795 until the present it has been held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Fragmenta Mosquensia were brought to Moscow in 1665. They were examined by Matthaei.The last was Porphyrius Uspensky, who took one leaf from the monastery. The codex is now located in eight places, in seven libraries, in six cities in Europe. Contains: Contains: 1 Corinthians 10:22-29, 11:9-16; 2 Corinthians 4:2-7, 10:5-11:8, 11:12-12:4; Galatians 1:1-10, 2:9-17, 4:30-5:5; Colossians 1:26-2:8, 2:20-3:11; 1 Thessalonians 2:9-13, 4:5-11; 1 Timothy 1:7-2:13, 3:7-13, 6:9-13; 2 Timothy 2:1-9; Titus 1:1-3, 1:15-2:5, 3:13-15; Hebrews 1:3-8, 2:11-16, 3:13-18, 4:12-15, 10:1-7, 10:32-38, 12:10-15, 13:24-25

title: Uncial 073
description: It was found by Rendel Harris, who edited its text. The codex 073 is located now in Saint Catherine's Monastery in the Sinai Peninsula (Sinai Harris 7), and the codex 084 in the Russian National Library (Gr. 277, 1f) in Saint Petersburg. Contains: Matthew 14:28-31

title: Uncial 0279
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. It is a palimpsest, the upper text was written in Greek, in uncial letters, and contains liturgical texts. Contains: Luke 8:32-44, 22:2-3, 15–16

title: Uncial 0280
description: It is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: Hebrews 9:14-18

title: Uncial 0281
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. It is a palimpsest, the upper text contains part of the Old Testament. Contains: Matthew 6–27

title: Codex Tischendorfianus II
description: Codex Tischendorfianus II a.k.a. 0285. It is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery at Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. This manuscript was part of the same codex to which Uncial 081 belonged. Contains: Romans 5:12, 14, 8:37-9:5, 13:1-4, 13:11-14:3; 1 Corinthians 4:2-7, 12:16, 18, 21-30, 14:26-33; Ephesians 3:13-20, 5:28-6:1; 1 Timothy 1:1-7; Hebrews 8:9-9:1, 9:25-10:2, 11:3-7, 12:22-13:25; 1 Peter 3:17-4:1

title: Uncial 0286
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: Matthew 16:13-19; John 10:12-16

title: Uncial 0287
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: Matthew 1-8; 21; 22,1-3; Mark 16:19; Luke 1-12; John 2; 10; 12; 13; 17; 20; 21.

title: Uncial 0288
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. It is a palimpsest, the upper text is in Greek written by minuscule hand, it contains part of the Old Testament. Contains: Luke 5:33-34.36-37; 5:39-6:1.3-4

title: Uncial 0289
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. It is a palimpsest, the upper text is in Greek written by minuscule hand, it contains part of Old Testament. Contains: Romans 8:19-21.32-35; 1 Corinthians 2:11-4:12; 13:13-14:1.3-11.13-19

title: Uncial 0290
description: This Greek-Arabic diglot is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. The text was published by L. Politis in 1980. Contains: John 18:4-20:2

title: Uncial 0291
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: Gospel of Luke 8:45-9:2

title: Uncial 0292
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: Mark 6:55-7:5

title: Uncial 0294
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: Book of Acts 14:27-15:10

title: Uncial 0295
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: 2 Corinthians 12:14-13:1

title: Uncial 0296
description: This is one of the manuscripts discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai in May 1975, during restoration work. Currently the codex is still housed at the monastery. Contains: 1 John 5:3-13; 2 Corinthians 7:3-4.9-10

title: Uncial 094
description: It was discovered in Saloniki. Contains: Matthew 24:9–21

title: Uncial 0115
description: The codex was adapted to the Church use, but it is not a Lectionary. This fragment was brought to light by Scholz. It was at the end of another book. The text was published by Constantin von Tischendorf in Monumenta sacra inedita (1846). Contains: Gospel of Luke 9-10

title: Uncial 0321
description: Probably it was brought from Sinai by Constantin von Tischendorf. Gregory catalogued it as Uncial 067 on his list. After re-examination made by Pasquale Orsini it is clear that it is different manuscript. In 2010 it was catalogued by the INTF separately as 0321. The manuscript was examined by Tischendorf, who edited its text in 1846. It was also examined and described by Eduard de Muralt,[8] Kurt Treu,[9] and recently by Pasquale Orsini. It is currently housed at the Russian National Library (Suppl. Gr. 6 III, fol. 10-12) in Saint Petersburg. It is a palimpsest, the upper text was written in the 10th century in Georgian language it contains calendar. Contains: Matthew 20:2–17

title: Uncial 067
description: Probably it was brought from Sinai. It is a palimpsest, the upper text was written in the 10th century it contains Georgian calendar. Contains: Matthew 14:13-16.19-23; 24:37-25:1.32-45; 26:31-45; Mark 9:14-22; 14:58-70.

title: Sinaiticus
description: Discovered in Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai by Constantin Tischendorf, when he went there in May 1844. Contains: New Testament

title: Uncial 0140
description: The codex now is located in Saint Catherine's Monastery. Contains: Acts 2:45-3:8

title: Uncial 0136
description: Greek-Arabic diglot. The codex was taken from Sinai and now is located in the National Library of Russia in Saint Petersburg. The manuscript 0136 was part of the same codex to which Uncial 0137 belonged. They were divided in the 19th century and catalogued under different numbers. Uncial 0137 is still located in Sinai Harris 9 in the Saint Catherine's Monastery in Mount Sinai in Egypt. Contains: Matthew 14:6-13, 25:9-16, 25:41-26:1

title: Uncial 0108
description: Constantin von Tischendorf brought the manuscript from the East in 1859, and edited its text in his Notitia. Contains: Luke 11:37-45

title: Uncial 0189
description: Uncial 0189 is the oldest parchment manuscript of the New Testament. Uncial 0189 is an important early witness to the Alexandrian text-type, nearly always agreeing with the other witnesses to this type of text. A transcription of the text of Uncial 0189 was first published by Aarne H. Salonius in Zeitschrift für die neutestamentliche Wissenschaft in 1927. Contains: Acts 5:3–21

title: Uncial 0213
description: The manuscript was added to the list of the New Testament manuscripts by Kurt Aland in 1953. Contains: Mark 3:2-3, 5

title: Athous Dionysiou
description: The codex is now located at the Dionysiou monastery, on Mount Athos. Contains: Gospels

title: Athous Lavrensis
description: The manuscript was seen by biblical scholar Caspar René Gregory on August 26, 1886. He described it as the first of its kind. In 1892, the biblical scholar J. Rendel Harris did not examine the codex even though he was on a visit to Mount Athos, as he was only inspecting the Septuagint (an early Greek translation of the Old Testament) manuscripts there. Contains: Gospels (lacking Matthew 1:1-Mark 9:5), Acts, Pauline Epistles (lacking Hebrews 8:11-9:19), General Epistles

title: Basilensis
description: a.k.a. Codex Basilensis A. N. III. 12 or Ee or Uncial 07. It was probably brought to Basel by Cardinal Ragusio (1380–1443),[3] who may have acquired it in Constantinople when he attended the Council of Florence in 1431.[5]: 131  In 1559 it was presented to the monastery of the Preaching Friars.[3] In the same year it was transferred to Basel University Library (shelf number A. N. III. 12), in Basel (Switzerland). The manuscript contains marginal notes, was adapted for liturgical reading, and contains some missing portions. Three leaves of the codex were overwritten by a later hand; these leaves are considered palimpsests. It was probably brought to Basel by Cardinal Ragusio (1380–1443), who may have acquired it in Constantinople when he attended the Council of Florence in 1431. In 1559 it was presented to the monastery of the Preaching Friars. Though it was available for biblical scholar Desiderius Erasmus for his edition of the first published printed Greek New Testament, he never consulted it. The text of the manuscript was collated by textual critic Johann Jakob Wettstein,[15] and the manuscript was used by John Mill in his edition of the Greek New Testament. It has been cited in printed editions of the Greek New Testament since the 18th century. The manuscript is cited in nearly all critical editions of the Greek New Testament, except the NA27. Contains: Gospels

title: Codex Koridethi
description: A.k.a. Codex Coridethianus. Found in a monastery in Koridethi (Caucasus region, near the Black Sea). The Greek text of the Gospel of Matthew chapters 1-14, and the whole of the Gospel of Luke and Gospel of John is considered to be more or less a representative of the Byzantine text-type, while the text of the Gospel of Mark has been considered to be a representative of the Caesarean text-type. It is commonly believed the manuscript is named after the town in which it was discovered; however, this is not correct. The first publication of the entire manuscript by Beermann and Gregory states: Kala/Caucasia: In the year 1853 a certain Bartholomeé visited a long abandoned monastery in Kala, a little village in the Caucasian mountains near the Georgian/Russian border (some miles south east of the 5600m high Elbrus). There, in an old church, far off every civilisation, he discovered the MS. The MS rested there probably for several hundred years (Beermann: ca. 1300–1869). Koridethi: Before this time the MS was in a town called Koridethi. This was a village near the Black Sea, near today's Batumi in Georgia. There should still be some ruins of a monastery. Notes in the Gospel indicate dates from ca. 965 CE on. At around this time, according to a note, the book has been rebound. The book was there until around 1300 CE. Further south, Armenia: A Greek inscription mentions the city of Tephrice or Tephrike (Τεφρική): "I, Kurines, Comes of the comandant of the city Tephrice came to the castelles and went back to the fort of the Great Martyrs(?)." Even though the content and meaning is not completely clear, the city Tephrice is clear. The town was destroyed in 873. It was on a line between today's Sivas and Malatya in Turkey/Armenia. Beermann's conclusion therefore is (p. 581) that the codex must be older than 873 CE. Beermann speculates that the "fort of the Great Martyrs" (if correctly deciphered) might have been Martyropolis, a town near the Wan Lake, near today's Batman in Turkey. The codex is now located in Tbilisi, at the Georgian National Center of Manuscripts, Gr. 28. Contains: Gospels

title: Ephraemi Rescriptus
description: Exact location of origin is unknown, possibly Egypt, but we know it was brought from Constantinople to Florence in 1453. Contains: New Testament

title: Guelferbytanus A
description: Formerly the manuscript was held in Bobbio, Weissenburg, Mainz, and Prague. The Duke of Brunswick bought it in 1689. The manuscript became known to scholars in the latter half of the 18th century. Franz Anton Knittel (1721–1792) discovered it in the Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel. Contains: Gospels

title: Guelferbytanus B
description: The manuscript was discovered in the 18th century by Franz Anton Knittel (1721–1792) in the Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel. Contains: Luke, John

title: Monacensis
description: A.k.a. X 033. The early history of the codex is unknown. Its known history begins with Dutch professor Gerhard Voss, who donated it to a Jesuit college in Ingolstadt, Germany. It was later held in Innsbruck before arriving at its final location in Munich in 1827. The manuscript was heavily studied throughout the 18th and 19th centuries. Contains: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.

title: Mosquensis I
description: The manuscript came from the Dionysiou monastery at Athos to Moscow in 1655. Contains: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude

title: Mosquensis II
description: The manuscript was previously held in the Vatopedi monastery an Mount Athos, Greece. In 1655 it was brought by the monk Arsenius to Moscow, on the suggestion of the Patriarch Nikon, in the reign of Alexei Mikhailovich Romanov (1645–1676).It was collated by Matthaei in 1779 and in 1783, at which time the manuscript was only missing the texts of Matthew 22:44-23:35, and John 21:10 to the end, with the now missing portions somehow being lost afterwards. According to biblical scholar Frederick H. A. Scrivener, it was one of the best manuscripts collated by Matthaei. Contains: Gospels

title: Petropolitanus
description: The manuscript belonged to the family Parodi in Smyrna. It was brought by Tischendorf in 1859. Contains: Gospels

title: Petropolitanus Purp.
description: The manuscript originated in the 6th-century imperial scriptorium of Constantinople. It was dismembered during the 12th-century crusades, which scattered its fragments to various locations, including London, Vienna, the Vatican, and Patmos. In 1896, the largest portion was purchased for the Imperial Public Library in St. Petersburg. Numerous scholars, including Wettstein and Tischendorf, studied the separate fragments over the centuries. A complete facsimile of all known pieces was published in 2002, and a significant academic study was published by Elijah Hixson in 2019. Contains: Gospels

title: Regius
description: The early history of the manuscript is unknown. The codex is now located in the National Library of France, in Paris. Contains: Gospels

title: Rossanensis
description: The early history of the manuscript is unknown. Several theories have been provided, with a suggestion that it came in the 7th century CE, along with Basilian monks, from either Constantinople, Egypt, or from after the Islamic conquest of north Africa. Another theory claims that it arrived when Rossano became a Diocese in the X century, marking the moment of highest splendor for the city. It was discovered in 1846 in Rossano Cathedral, the Rossano Gospels is the oldest extant illuminated manuscript of the New Testament Gospels. The Gospels were written after the Ostrogoths of the Byzantine Empire recaptured the Italian peninsula after the war (from 535 to 553). The manuscript was rediscovered in 1879 in the sacristy of Rossano Cathedral by Oskar von Gebhardt and Adolf Harnack. On 9 October 2015 in Abu Dhabi, UNESCO inscribed the Codex Purpureus Rossanensis in its Memory of the World international register. Although it is no longer used in Christian ceremonies, this particular type of Gospel codex is important for dissecting art and symbolism, and research on the pages has shed light on early Christian beliefs.The manuscript has been dated by the Institute for New Testament Textual Research (INTF) to the 6th century. Contains: Matthew, Mark

title: Sangallensis
description: The earliest history of the manuscript is unknown, however it is likely that it was written in the West, possibly by an Irish monk in the St. Gallen monastery at some point during the 9th century.[4]: 87  It can not be dated earlier, because it has a reference to the (heretical) opinions of Gottschalk of Orbais (died 868) at Luke 13:24 and John 12:40. Contains: Gospels

title: Seidelianus I
description: A.k.a. Codex Wolfii A and Codex Harleianus. The codex was brought from the East to Germany by scholar Andrew Erasmus Seidel ( 1718). After his death in 1718, it was acquired by Maturin Veyssière de La Croze, the royal librarian in Berlin, and presented to Johann Christoph Wolf,[7][8] who published extracts from its text in 1723.  The codex was barbarously mutilated in 1721 in order to send pieces to Bentley. Most of them were purchased by Eduard Harley. Some fragments were found by biblical scholar Samuel P. Tregelles in 1845. It later became part of the library of Edward Harley, and is now located in the British Library, except one page, which Wolff gave to Richard Bentley, is in Cambridge Contains: Gospels

title: Seidelianus II
description: The codex was brought from the East by Erasmus Seidel at the beginning of the 17th century, together with Codex Seidelianus I. Maturin Veyssière de La Croze bought it 1718, in the same time as Seidelianus I.Since 1838 the codex is located in Hamburg Universitätsbibliothek. One leaf of the codex is housed at Trinity College, Cambridge. Contains: Gospels

title: Sinopensis
description: The codex was purchased in 1899 at Sinope (hence its name), by a French officer, from an old Greek woman. The style of illustrations suggests Syria or Palestine (even Mesopotamia) as the place of its origin. Contains: Gospel of Matthew

title: Tischendorfianus III
description: The codex was held at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in Egypt and was found by Constantin von Tischendorf in 1853, who took away only the uncial text (Luke-John) — along with Codex Tischendorfianus IV — and brought it to the Bodleian Library in Oxford, where it is now located. The place of origin is still speculative. According to Gregory it is possible that the manuscript was written and corrected in Jerusalem. It is very difficult to prove, but Palestine is still shown as one of the possible places. Nothing is known of the early history of the codex until its discovery by Tischendorf. Contains: Luke, John
location: St. Catherine's Monastery, Mt. Sinai, Egypt

title: Tischendorfianus IV
description: Uncial 036, a.k.a. Codex Tischendorfianus IV. One part of the codex was found by Tischendorf in an eastern monastery in 1853, another part in 1859. Contains: Gospels

title: Tischendorfianus I
description: Codex Tischendorfianus I, a.k.a Uncial 0106, brought by Constantin von Tischendorf in 1845 and in 1853 from Sinai. Tischendorf edited its text in Monumenta sacra inedita. From the same manuscript originated four other leaves now catalogued as Uncial 0119. It was discovered by J. Rendel Harris at Sinai, who examined it. Hermann von Soden designed it as ε 63. It is still housed in the Saint Catherine's Monastery (Sinai Harris 8, 56,8 ff.) on the Sinai peninsula. Contains: Matthew 13:37-46, 13:55-14:8, 14:29-15:4, 15:15-26

title: Uncial 0121
description: The manuscript was examined by Johann Jakob Griesbach. Griesbach was the first who observed similarities between Londoner fragment (0121a) and Hamburger fragment (0121b), and supposed that they came from the same manuscript.The codex is located in the British Library in London. It was classified with Uncial 0121b as the same manuscript, but it is now established that they belonged to different manuscripts. Contains: 1 Corinthians 15:52-2 Corinthians 1:15; 10:13-12:5

title: Uncial 0212
description: A.k.a. Dura Parchment 24. Found in Dura Europos (a Roman border town in modern-day Syria); found in 1933. Its origin is not certain, it was found in the ruins of a city destroyed in A.D. 256. Possibly the only surviving manuscript of the Greek Diatessaron, it is not, strictly speaking, a manuscript of the New Testament — it contains only phrases from the text of the Gospels. Generally, it has been regarded as a fragment of Tatian's Diatessaron (Gospel harmony). On March 5, 1933, during the excavations conducted by Clark Hopkins amongst the ruins of a Roman border-town, Dura-Europos, on the lower Euphrates, under the embankment which filled in the street inside the wall and also covered the Christian church and the Jewish synagogue, the parchment fragment now known as Dura Parchment 24 was found. Susan M. Hopkins was the first to recognize it as a portion of the Gospel. Contains: Matthew 27:56–57; Mark 15:40,42; Luke 23:49,50,51; John 19:38

title: Uncial 0250
description: A.k.a. Codex Climaci Rescriptus. GA 0250 is the Greek layer of a collective palimpsest, overwritten by the Syriac treatises of John Climacus — the Scala Paradisi and the Liber ad Pastorem — hence the codex name. The Greek section (CCR 5 & 6) contains the four Gospels with extensive lacunae on 34 parchment folios (23 x 15.5 cm), two columns per page, 31 lines per page, in uncial letters, assigned palaeographically to the 7th or 8th century. Ian A. Moir suggested it preserves a substantial record of an early Greek uncial Gospel manuscript once at Caesarea, a sister of Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, now otherwise lost; Moir edited the Greek text. Gregory originally catalogued it as lectionary 1561. The manuscript originates from Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, per the New Finds of 1975. One folio was bought by Agnes Smith Lewis in Cairo in 1895, 89 more came from an undisclosed Berlin scholar in 1905, and 48 further folios were acquired at Port Tewfik in 1906; Lewis and Margaret Gibson later donated the bulk to Westminster College, Cambridge. After failing to sell at Sotheby's in 2009, it was bought in 2010 by Steve Green and now resides in the Green Collection, with one folio in the Mingana Collection, Birmingham, and eight in the library at Saint Catherine's Monastery. The remaining layers of the codex are not part of GA 0250: eight Christian Palestinian Aramaic manuscripts of the 5th-6th century on 112 folios, including Gospels, Acts, the Epistles, portions of the Old Jerusalem lectionary, and the apocryphal Dormition of the Mother of God — the second largest early CPA corpus after Codex Sinaiticus Rescriptus, edited by Agnes Smith Lewis and re-edited by Christa Müller-Kessler and Michael Sokoloff. In 2021 parts of the lost star catalogue of Hipparchus of Nicaea were identified in the manuscript. Contains: Gospels† (Matthew 2:12-27:40; Mark 14:72-15:28; Luke 22:60-23:38; John 6:53-21:1)"
location: St. Catherine's Monastery, Mt. Sinai, Egypt

title: Uncial 0319
description: A.k.a. Codex Sangermanensis, is a tenth-century diglot manuscript, formerly in the library of St. Germain des Prés, Paris, hence its name Sangermanensis, "of Saint Germanus". It is particularly notable as one of the two such copies which display clear evidence of having had Claromontanus as exemplar. It is a diglot, including the Vetus Latina translation. The manuscript was written by Latin scribe, who may have been unfamiliar with Greek. The manuscript was examined and described by Bernard de Montfaucon, Johann Jakob Wettstein, Giuseppe Bianchini, and Johann Jakob Griesbach, who designated it by siglum E. In 1805 it was collated by Matthaei. The manuscript was held in the St. Germain des Prés at Paris. The St. Germain Library suffered severely during the French Revolution, and Peter Dubrovsky, Secretary to the Russian Embassy at Paris, acquired this manuscript together with many other manuscripts stolen from the ecclesiastical libraries. Contains: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews

title: Codex Vaticanus 2066
description: a.k.a. Uncial 046, formerly known as Codex Basilianus. The manuscript was once owned by Philippo Vitali (1590–1653), first published by Cardinal Angelo Mai in 1859. A 10th-century Greek uncial manuscript written on vellum, though some scholars have proposed earlier dates. In addition to the complete text of the Book of Revelation, it contains non-biblical homilies by Basil the Great and others. Contains: Revelation

title: Codex Vaticanus Graecus 2061
description: A.k.a. Uncial 048. Formerly it was held in the monastery of St. Mary of Patirium, a suburb of Rossano in Calabria, whence it was taken about the end of the 17th century to the Vatican. Here it was rediscovered by Pierre Batiffol in 1887. It contains parts of the New Testament, homilies of several authors, and Strabo's Geographica. Formerly it was known also as the Codex Basilianus 100, earlier as Codex Patriniensis 27.[1] It was designated by ב a, p. It is a double palimpsest containing parts of seven different literary works. They are written in several types of uncial script. The oldest text is from the 5th century, the youngest from the 10th century. Contains: Acts 26:6-27:4, 28:3-31; James 4:14-5:20; 1 Peter 1:1-12; 2 Peter 2:4-8, 2:13-3:15; 1 John 4:6-5:13, 5:17-18,5:21; 2 John; 3 John; Romans 13:4-15:9; 1 Corinthians 2:1-3:11, 3:22, 4:4-6,5:5-11, 6:3-11,12:23-15:17, 15:20-27; 2 Corinthians 4:7-6:8, 8:9-18,8:21-10:6; Ephesians 5:8-end; Philippians 1:8-23, 2:1-4, 2:6-8; Colossians 1:2-2:8, 2:11-14, 22–23,3:7-8, 3:12-4:18; 1 Thessalonians 1:1, 5–6, 1 Timothy 5:6-6:17, 6:20-21, 2 Timothy 1:4-6, 1:8, 2:2-25; Titus 3:13-end; Philemon; Hebrews 11:32-13:4

title: Vaticanus 354
description: Formerly known as Codex Guelpherbytanus. The name of the scribe was Michael, a monk, who finished his work "in the month of March, the fifth day, the sixth hour, the year 6457, the seventh indiction". The manuscript was examined and described by Bianchini, in the 1700s. Contains: Gospels

title: Alexandrinus
description: Place of origin is unknown, Alexandria is the traditional view and considered most probable. there is a note written in the manuscript from Athanasius III, who was patriarch of Alexandria from 1276 to 1316. Brought to Constantinople in 1621 and presented to King James I in 1624. Contains: New Testament

title: Angelicus

title: Augiensis
description: Codex Augiensis is named after the monastery of Augia Dives in Lake Constance. In 1718 Richard Bentley (1662–1742) was its owner. Contains: Pauline epistles (lacking Romans 1:1-3:19, 1 Cor. 3:8-16, 6:7-14, Col. 2:1-8, Philem. 21-25, Hebrews)

title: Beratinus
description: Codex Purpureus Beratinus. Formerly it was believed to have been at Patmos. According to Xhevat Lloshi it came from Ballsh. It was held in Berat, Albania from 1356. The text of the codex was published by Pierre Batiffol in 1887. "During World War II, Hitler learned of it and sought it out. Several monks and priests risked their lives to hide the manuscript." Since 1971, it has been preserved at the National Archives of Albania in Tirana. Contains: Matthew, Mark

title: Bezae
description: A.k.a. Codex Bezae Cantabrigiensis. Place of origin is unkown, believed to have been repaired at Lyon, France, in the ninth century, since it uses a distinctive kind of ink, acquired by Theodore Beza in 1562 and given to the University of Cambridge in 1581. Contains: Gospels, Acts

title: Borgianus
description: The manuscript came from the White Monastery. It once belonged to Cardinal Stefano Borgia, hence the name of the codex. Fragments of the codex were discovered independently at separate times and were numbered 029, 0113, 0125, and 0139. Together they have 23 leaves. "It appears that the ignorant monk who brought this manuscript with him from Egypt to Europe, was so unaware of its value, that he lost the greater part of the leaves". Contains: John

title: Campianus
description: The earliest history of the manuscript is unknown. It was called Campianus after the Abbott François de Camps, who gave it to King Louis XIV of France.The year in which this occurred is muddled, as the earliest scholar to note this (Ludolph Kuster) says it was presented in 1607; however this is an impossibility due to King Louis XIV not being born until 1638. Biblical scholars Tischendorf, Caspar René Gregory and Samuel P. Tregelles give the date as 1706, but Scrivener gives it as 1707. Contains: Gospels

title: Laudianus
description: It was probably written in Sardinia, during the Byzantine occupation, and therefore after 534 (terminus a quo). It was written before 716 (terminus ad quem), as it was used by Beda Venerabilis in his Expositio Actuum Apostolorum Retractata. It was brought to England probably by Theodore of Tarsus, Archbishop of Canterbury, in 668, or by Ceolfrid, Abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow, in the early part of the eighth century. It was probably deposited in one of the great monasteries in the north of England." It probably came to the continent with English missionaries in the 8th century and came into the possession of Hornbach Abbey in the Rhineland. In the Thirty Years' War, it came into the possession of William Laud, who donated the manuscript to the Bodleian Library in Oxford in 1636. Contains: Acts

title: Macedoniensis
description: The earliest history of the manuscript is unknown. The codex was acquired by stockbroker Joseph Bevan Braithwaite from Macedonia in 1901. A.k.a. Macedonianus. Contains: Gospels

title: Mutinensis
description: The manuscript was examined by Scholz (1794 – 1852), and again by Tischendorf in 1843 and Tregelles in 1846. Contains: Acts

title: Nanianus
description: Codex Nanianus, a.k.a. Uncial 030. The codex is named after its last owner, Giovanni Nanni (1432–1502).[3] It was described by Giovanni Luigi Mingarelli. The first person to collate its text was Friedrich Münter (1761–1830), who sent some extracts from its text to textual critic Andreas Birch. Birch used these extracts in his edition of the text of the four Gospels in Greek. The text of the manuscript was independently collated by textual critic and manuscript hunter Constantin von Tischendorf in 1843, and by biblical scholar Samuel P. Tregelles in 1846. ' It contains the Epistle to Carpius (a letter by the early Church Father Eusebius outlying his Gospel division and harmony system), the Eusebian tables at the beginning of the manuscript, the tables of contents (also known as κεφάλαια) before each Gospel, and subscriptions at the end of each Gospel. Before the Gospel of Mark it has a picture with the baptism of Jesus; before the Gospel of John it has a picture of John standing with the rays from the clouds above, and Prochorus (mentioned in the book of Acts) writing. Contains: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
